slides.1: Good morning. Poverty is not always far away. Look around: a classmate skips lunch, a family works long hours, a student has no quiet place to study.
slides.2: Goal one asks every country to end poverty in all its forms. That is not only about income. It is health care, housing, education, and a fair chance to start again.
slides.3: Look at Taiwan. We have good schools and new technology, but not every family feels safe. Some struggle with rent, some with medical bills, some with jobs that never last.
slides.4: Here is the first problem: working poverty. People work hard and still cannot feel safe. Short contracts, low pay and long hours break their plans, and worried parents have less time for their children.
slides.5: Rent is the next weight. When it is high, families spend less on food, books and buses. Students move house often or share a crowded room, and a noisy home is hard to study in.
slides.6: Poverty also shows up online. Some students have fast internet, a laptop and parents who can help. Others share one phone, so a digital gap slowly turns into a learning gap.
slides.7: Taiwan does have safety nets: social help, health insurance, emergency money and local offices. They protect our basic needs. But does that help arrive before a small problem turns into a crisis?
slides.8: Schools can soften the blow. Free meals, scholarships, counseling and after-school classes all help. A teacher who notices one quiet child early can change that child's whole year.
slides.9: Community groups help too. Food banks, social workers, religious groups and NGOs find the people that big systems miss. But gifts alone are not enough, because people also need skills.
slides.10: So what can we do? First, we can learn about money. Students can plan a budget, save a little, borrow with care, and learn how to spot a scam.
slides.11: Data can help as well. Students can map what is missing near them: food, buses, care for old people, classes after school. But data should guide our kindness, not replace it.
slides.12: Service learning turns ideas into action. Students can visit a local group, write posters in two languages, or teach younger children. We learn most when we work beside people.
slides.13: Taiwan is growing older fast. Many old people live alone and need care, money, a bus, and help with their phone. Poverty follows health and family, not only pay.
slides.14: Migrant workers and new immigrant families also need a fair door in. Language, forms and customs can make help hard to reach. When a service is clear, whole families can join in.
slides.15: Climate makes poverty worse. Floods and heat hurt low-income homes hardest, because they have fewer savings and fewer choices. So climate action is poverty action too.
slides.16: Now, dignity. Help should never make a person feel small. If we only see weakness, we miss the strength that is already there, so we should listen first.
slides.17: To sum up, this goal is about shared safety. Poverty touches school, health, a home and a dream. Taiwan already helps, but help must come sooner and reach further.
slides.18: We also need to drop the blame. Low pay, high prices, illness, caring for family, a flood: these push people down. Blaming is easy, and understanding is useful.
slides.19: Young people are not too small to act. Learn English and share these ideas, use data to show the problem, join a group near you. Together, small actions grow.
slides.20: So let's start where we stand. See poverty clearly, speak about it with respect, and act inside our own school. A fair future begins with what we choose to notice today.
